subject: chemistry
question_text: Discuss the similarities among the alkaline earth metals and the gradation in their electronic configuration.

mark_split.label: The elements and the general configuration

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Physics and Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.93, chapter 7 s-BLOCK ELEMENTS, LONG ANSWER QUESTIONS question 52(i). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. This book prints no exam-appearance years for this chapter, so appearances[] is empty — the chapter has long been examined, we simply have no sourced years for this question. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. SCOPE: question 52 is printed as one question with three parts and this card answers part (i) only, the electronic configuration. Parts (ii) and (iii), the hydration enthalpies and the oxides and hydroxides, are answered on their own cards; nothing here is repeated there. THE SIX CONFIGURATIONS WERE CHECKED AGAINST THE ATOMIC NUMBERS: Be 4 = [He]2s², Mg 12 = [Ne]3s², Ca 20 = [Ar]4s², Sr 38 = [Kr]5s², Ba 56 = [Xe]6s², Ra 88 = [Rn]7s². The two complete configurations written out in full were also checked: Mg = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s² is 12 electrons and Ca = 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s² is 20 electrons. A SOURCE-BOOK CORRECTION IS RELEVANT HERE AND IS RESPECTED: elsewhere the volume states that the alkaline earth metals possess a stronger electropositive nature than the alkali metals. They are LESS electropositive than the alkali metals, because removing two electrons costs far more than removing one; within group 2 the electropositive character does increase down the group. This card writes it that way. THE TWO ELECTRONS ARE REMOVED SUCCESSIVELY, not simultaneously, and the card now says so: the second ionisation enthalpy is larger than the first, which is a statement about a second, separate removal. CARRIED AS EXTRA CONTENT, to be confirmed by a teacher: the statement that the extra lattice and hydration enthalpy of the doubly charged ion outweighs the second ionisation enthalpy, which is why M⁺ is never seen, the statement that a group 2 atom is smaller than the group 1 atom of the same period, and the statement that the second ionisation enthalpy is always larger than the first.

insider_note: The question asks for similarities AND gradation, so an answer that gives only the ns² configuration has answered half of it; the trends in size and ionisation enthalpy are the other half.

steps.label: The elements and the general configuration
steps.mark_note: The elements and the ns² form
lines: The alkaline earth metals are the
elements of group 2: beryllium Be,
magnesium Mg, calcium Ca, strontium Sr,
barium Ba and radium Ra.
Each of them has TWO electrons in the
outermost s orbital, over a complete
noble gas core:
This one shared configuration is the
reason all six are placed in group 2
and the reason they behave alike.
The outermost shell decides the
chemistry, so the same outer shell
means the same chemistry.
steps.why: The question asks for the similarities first, and the ns² configuration is the similarity every other one comes from. Naming all six elements before the general form shows the pattern holds across the whole group and not merely for the two or three that are usually quoted.
common_mistakes: Writing ns¹ for the alkaline earth metals. That is the alkali metal configuration; group 2 is ns².
Leaving out beryllium or radium. Both belong to group 2, and beryllium is the first member.
Writing ns²np¹. There is no p electron in the outer shell of a group 2 atom in its ground state.
steps.memory_tip: Two outer electrons each: group 2 is ns² all the way down.
steps.margin_note: Name the six elements, then write the general form on its own line.

steps.label: The configurations written out
lines: Written in full for two of them:
Only the value of n changes down the
group. The ns² part never changes.
steps.why: Writing the configurations out is the evidence for the claim made above, and it also shows where the gradation comes from: n rises by one at each step because a new shell is being started, and everything that changes down the group follows from that.
common_mistakes: Writing Mg as 1s²2s²2p⁶3s¹. Magnesium has 12 electrons, so the outer shell is 3s².
Writing Ca as [Ar]3d². The 4s orbital fills before 3d, so calcium is [Ar]4s².
steps.memory_tip: The number in front of s climbs by one each step; the s² stays.
steps.margin_note: Two of the six written out in full are enough to show the pattern.

steps.label: Loss of the two electrons
lines: Both ns² electrons are removed, one
after the other, to give the M²⁺ ion:
The ion M²⁺ is left with the noble gas
configuration before it, a stable
arrangement.
The second electron costs more energy to
remove than the first, but the lattice
enthalpy and the hydration enthalpy
released by the doubly charged ion more
than make up for it. That is why M⁺ is
never seen and +2 is the only state.
Every alkaline earth metal therefore:
1. is divalent and shows only the +2
oxidation state,
2. is electropositive, though less so
than the alkali metal beside it,
3. forms compounds that are mostly ionic.
Beryllium is the exception to point 3.
Its compounds are largely covalent.
steps.why: This is where the shared configuration becomes shared chemistry. The two electrons are removed one after the other, and although the second costs more energy than the first, the doubly charged ion releases far more lattice and hydration enthalpy than the singly charged one, so no other oxidation state is seen anywhere in the group. Beryllium is named as the exception here because its ion is so small that it pulls the anion's electrons back towards itself instead of transferring cleanly.
common_mistakes: Writing a +1 oxidation state for an alkaline earth metal. Both outer electrons are lost, so the state is +2.
Writing that the alkaline earth metals are more electropositive than the alkali metals. They are less electropositive, because removing two electrons costs much more than removing one.
Writing that beryllium compounds are ionic like the rest of the group. They are largely covalent.
steps.memory_tip: Both electrons come off, the second harder than the first, so the charge is always +2 and never +1.
steps.margin_note: Name beryllium as the exception here; it is the point the rest of the group is measured against.

steps.label: Gradation in atomic and ionic size
lines: Going down the group a new shell is
added at each element, so both the
atomic and the ionic radii increase:
The same order holds for the ions:
Each of these atoms is SMALLER than the
alkali metal atom of the same period,
because the nuclear charge is one unit
higher and pulls the shell in.
steps.why: The gradation half of the question begins here. The size trend has the same cause as in group 1, a new shell at each step, and the comparison across to group 1 is worth one line because it explains why every group 2 property that depends on size is more marked than the group 1 one.
common_mistakes: Writing that the radii decrease down the group. A new shell is added at each step, so they increase.
Writing that a group 2 atom is larger than the group 1 atom of the same period. It is smaller, because of the higher nuclear charge.
steps.memory_tip: A new shell each step down, so bigger; one more proton across, so smaller.
steps.margin_note: Give both orders, atoms and ions, then the one comparison with group 1.

steps.label: Gradation in ionisation enthalpy
steps.mark_note: Ionisation enthalpy falls down the group
lines: The first ionisation enthalpy decreases
down the group:
The outer electrons are further from the
nucleus and better screened at each
step, so less energy is needed.
The second ionisation enthalpy is always
larger than the first, because the
electron is being pulled off an ion that
already carries a positive charge.
These values are higher than those of
the alkali metals of the same periods.
steps.why: The second half of the gradation has the same explanation as the first: distance from the nucleus and screening. Saying that the second ionisation enthalpy exceeds the first, and that both exceed the group 1 values, is what shows why these metals are less electropositive than their group 1 neighbours even though they still form ions readily.
common_mistakes: Writing that ionisation enthalpy increases down the group. It decreases.
Writing that the second ionisation enthalpy is smaller than the first. Removing an electron from a positive ion always takes more energy.
steps.memory_tip: Down the group the electrons get easier to remove; the second one is always harder than the first.
steps.margin_note: Both statements belong here: the trend down the group and the first against the second.

steps.label: The conclusion

lines.text: All alkaline earth metals are ns²

lines: The shared ns² configuration is the
similarity, and it gives every member
the same +2 state.
The steady rise in size and the steady
fall in ionisation enthalpy down the
group are the gradation.
Together they are what makes these six
elements one group.
steps.why: The question named two things, similarities and gradation, so the closing lines have to name both and say which is which. The similarity is the configuration itself; the gradation is what happens to size and ionisation enthalpy as n increases.
common_mistakes: Answering only the similarities. The question asks for the gradation as well.
Ending at the last trend with no closing statement. One sentence tying the two halves together completes the answer.
steps.memory_tip: Same ns² is the similarity; the steady change in size and ionisation enthalpy is the gradation.
steps.margin_note: Close by naming both halves the question asked for, in that order.
